title: The Forest That Feeds the Rivers

pages.text: The Atewa range, in the Eastern Region of Ghana, is a green ridge of forest. According to conservation groups, it holds the headwaters of three rivers, the Ayensu, the Densu and the Birim, which supply water to more than five million people. The same groups report about three thousand plant species and more than five hundred and seventy kinds of butterfly there. Nelson, a school-magazine reporter, wanted to know why people were arguing about it.
sentences: The Atewa range, in the Eastern Region of Ghana, is a green ridge of forest.
According to conservation groups, it holds the headwaters of three rivers, the Ayensu, the Densu and the Birim, which supply water to more than five million people.
The same groups report about three thousand plant species and more than five hundred and seventy kinds of butterfly there.
Nelson, a school-magazine reporter, wanted to know why people were arguing about it.
pages.alt: A forested ridge with three streams flowing from it and a map beside it.

pages.text: His first interview was with Madam Sakyi, a conservationist. “The forest acts like a sponge,” she said. “It soaks up rain and releases it slowly into streams. If the forest is stripped or polluted, the rivers may suffer, and millions of people depend on them. Mining, especially illegal mining, has already spread into parts of the reserve, according to our group’s recent statement. We want it made a national park.”

We want it made a national park.”
pages.alt: A conservationist holds a map showing a forest with three rivers and mining pits marked.

pages.text: Nelson’s second interview was with Mr Awuah, a district official. “Bauxite is used to make aluminium,” he said. “The government has argued that mining Atewa’s bauxite could bring national revenue and jobs, and that new technology can limit damage. I must say that the plans have been debated for years, and there are serious objections. People should check the latest position. Meanwhile, reports say illegal miners have entered the reserve, and the national anti-illegal mining team has launched an operation, called Operation Green Shield, with arrests reported.” Nelson wrote down: official view, revenue and jobs, damage limited by technology, claim not agreed.

pages.text: Next he met Victor, who had worked in small-scale mining. “I am not a villain,” Victor said. “I left school, and there are no jobs. Gold pays quickly.” He looked at the ground. “But the river near us is brown, and my little brother got sick. If someone gave us a safe job, I would take it.” Nelson was quiet. “Thank you for being honest,” he said.

pages.text: Last, Nelson visited a village elder, who told him that the paramount chief of the area had said that he is committed to protecting the forest. “The forest is not only trees,” the elder said. “It is where our streams begin, our herbs grow and our ancestors rest.” Nelson wrote: chief’s position, protect the forest, as reported. He knew he must not put words in anybody’s mouth.

pages.text: Back at school, Nelson collected the claims on a board. Conservationists: a national park with eco-tourism and agroforestry could bring more than five million United States dollars a year and at least three thousand jobs. “That is their estimate,” he wrote. Government: mining could give revenue and jobs. “That is their claim.” Victor: no jobs and a dirty river. Elder: the forest is heritage and source. “Four voices,” said Nelson, “and none of them is a fool.”

pages.text: Mrs Ahiable, the English teacher, nodded. “A good writer does not pretend that a debate is simple,” she said. “Present the arguments for and against, give the facts you can check, admit what you do not know, and then give a reasoned conclusion.” Nelson sat and thought. “If the rivers are the source of water for millions,” he wrote, “then perhaps the forest is worth more standing than mined. But I will say that I am not an expert.”

pages.text: Nelson wrote: “The question of mining in a forest reserve has two sides. On the one hand, supporters argue that bauxite could bring revenue and jobs to a country that needs both. On the other hand, conservationists argue that the forest protects the headwaters of three rivers and shelters rare species. Both sides want a better Ghana. However, damage to a water source is hard to reverse. In conclusion, I believe that the forest should be protected while safe jobs are found for young people such as Victor.”

pages.alt: A boy writes a discursive essay at a desk with a map of the forest and rivers beside him.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a discursive essay looks at both sides before giving a conclusion. Use “on the one hand”, “on the other hand”, “however” and “in conclusion”, write in the present tense for opinions, and avoid contractions and slang. Nelson named each claim’s owner, such as “supporters” and “conservationists”, instead of presenting claims as facts. In your time, you may be one of the people who decides. Learn the facts first. The end.
